findings.assertion: INAH's indexed monument catalog describes an 1897 legislative-palace competition and names Boari, Burnam/Weber and Rivas Mercado as prize recipients before the French architect Émile Bénard's project was adopted; the visitor-operator narrative calls Bénard the winner. Record this as conflicting competition-result narratives, not a resolved winner.
findings.source_locator: INAH ficha I-0013801611 indexed historical paragraph versus MRM direct history lines 18–24
findings.limitations: Exact original 1897 jury decision, protest and Quaglia/Bénard commission contracts missing; catalog marked validation pending.

findings.assertion: The steel-framed federal legislative palace began construction circa 1906 under Bénard and the project was suspended circa 1912, leaving a central structural shell that survived revolutionary upheaval rather than a completed parliament.
findings.source_locator: MRM history lines 18–30; UNAM CCH teaching PDF later discussion of palace versus revolution architecture
findings.limitations: The exact 1912 stoppage date derives from operator chronology; original treasury work accounts and 1910 construction reports unexamined.

findings.assertion: Émile Bénard proposed reusing the unfinished structure as a revolutionary pantheon during the 1920s, before the Obregón Santacilia transformation of the 1930s. The memorial idea therefore was not a sudden invention unique to 1933.
findings.source_locator: MRM history lines 28–30: proposal to Álvaro Obregón; 1928 and 1929 deaths
findings.limitations: Date and documentary form of Bénard's proposal require original architectural correspondence and sketches.

findings.assertion: The 1930s rescue of the abandoned iron structure combined architectural intervention and political patronage; Angélica Vázquez del Mercado summarizes conflicting retrospective attributions of the proposal to Carlos Obregón Santacilia and finance minister Alberto J. Pani. The monument was completed in 1938.
findings.source_locator: Gaceta de Museos p.19 and notes 2–3, citing Pani memoir and Obregón account; MRM history lines 43–56; INAH indexed historical note
findings.limitations: Memoirs/1933 steel disposal documents and commission approvals not directly examined; no singular inventor attribution approved.

findings.assertion: A review of the monument's foundations after the 1985 earthquake revived the previously unrealized plan to convert underground areas into a museum; the Museo Nacional de la Revolución opened on 20 November 1986, and its history team under Eugenia Meyer emphasized social processes and ordinary participants rather than a hero-only narrative.
findings.source_locator: Gaceta de Museos pp.19–20, lines 19–35: foundation review, team and museum opening
findings.limitations: Original 1985 engineering assessment, 1986 inaugural exhibition inventory and complete institutional records not examined.

findings.assertion: The current monument preserves the central iron-framed former Salón de Pasos Perdidos of the never-completed Palacio Legislativo; after the 2010 redesign the site museum presented portions of this steel structure through windows. A guided walk could point visitors toward architectural reuse rather than describe all exposed iron as 1938 construction.
findings.source_locator: Gaceta de Museos p.22, lines 61–65: museum-site glazing and Bénard/Obregón/Oliverio; MRM lines 97–104
findings.limitations: 2026 displays/access and precisely which girders are visible not field-verified; 2010 description not assumed current.

findings.assertion: The four exterior sculptural groups attributed to Oliverio Martínez are arranged as Labor Laws (northwest pillar), Agrarian Laws (southwest), Independence (southeast), and Reform Laws (northeast). Operator descriptions identify a gear/hammer for workers and a sickle/property title for agrarian law; this can support concrete looking prompts once physical visibility is confirmed.
findings.source_locator: MRM direct history lines 62–85 detailed oriented groups; UNAM image-catalog indexed authorship
findings.limitations: Sculptural meaning reflects operator interpretation, not artist notes; original sculptor drawings and 2026 view angles unverified.

findings.assertion: Decorative objects commissioned for the aborted legislative palace were reused elsewhere: the operator lists the Juventud/Madurez marbles at Bellas Artes, an eagle at Monumento a la Raza, and lions at an entrance to Bosque de Chapultepec. This is a promising cross-city material-history route rather than a confirmed matched artifact itinerary.
findings.source_locator: MRM direct history lines 36–41 (three object groups and suggested destinations)
findings.limitations: Object accession records, individual attribution, exact entrance, current state and reproduction permissions unverified.

findings.assertion: The monument acquired its mausoleum role in 1936, before all currently commemorated revolutionaries were interred: the operator dates Carranza's transfer to 1942, Madero's to 1960, Calles's to 1969, Cárdenas's burial to 1970 and Villa's transfer to 1976. The timeline shows the revolutionary pantheon itself was assembled over decades.
findings.source_locator: MRM direct history lines 87–88, independently consistent broad outline in 2010 Notimex report
findings.limitations: Individual funeral decree originals, burial registries and contested identification of Villa's remains not checked; do not infer political unanimity.

findings.assertion: The monument operator identifies black Chimalhuacán volcanic stone as edge/base material and Chiluca quarry stone as surfaces, while UNAM's photographic catalog lists Chiluca technique for a sculpture; these are material descriptions at different object scales, not a single laboratory-petrographic identification of every stone.
findings.source_locator: MRM lines 49–53; UNAM AFMT IIE:AFMT:TE3566 indexed stone technique
findings.limitations: Original quarry invoices, petrography and component-by-component conservation surveys absent.

findings.assertion: The INAH Gaceta author cites an estimate of 17,000 foundation piles under the structure and describes a planned double dome; the operator contrasts the former internal lift and inter-dome ascending route with the central panoramic elevator installed during the 2009–2010 renovation. These are sources for a physical engineering narrative, not a verified structural survey.
findings.source_locator: Gaceta de Museos p.19 lines 7–12 and note 1 for 17,000-pile estimate; MRM lines 55–56 and 97–104 for lift routes; 2012 UNAM abstract for contested renovation
findings.limitations: 17,000 figure secondhand from 2009 publication; no pile drawings, engineering tests, elevator as-built or recent safety/access verification.
